title: The Carnian Pluvial Episode
evidenceNote: Rock layers of this age around the world switch from dry-climate to wet-climate sediments, and their chemistry points to huge eruptions.
text: For one to two million years the dry Triassic world turned much rainier. The trigger was probably huge volcanic eruptions off western North America (the Wrangellia lavas), which released carbon dioxide and warmed the climate. About a third of marine genera died out. Afterwards dinosaurs, conifers, modern-type corals and other groups that still shape today's world spread widely.

sources.title: Dal Corso et al. 2020, Science Advances: Extinction and dawn of the modern world in the Carnian

title: Ischigualasto: the oldest dinosaurs
place: Ischigualasto Provincial Park, San Juan, Argentina
evidenceNote: Layers of volcanic ash between the fossil beds contain radioactive minerals that give their age.
text: The 'Valley of the Moon' in north-west Argentina holds some of the oldest known dinosaurs, including Eoraptor and Herrerasaurus. They lived on a volcanically active river plain with strongly seasonal rain. Dinosaurs were still a minor part of the fauna: most of the bones belong to other reptiles and to cynodonts, the relatives of mammals.

sources.title: UC Museum of Paleontology: Ischigualasto Formation, Argentina
UC Museum of Paleontology: The Triassic Period

title: Ghost Ranch and Coelophysis
evidenceNote: The skeletons lie in Late Triassic river sediments whose age is known from their fossils and from dated rock layers in the same region.
text: In 1947 a quarry at Ghost Ranch yielded hundreds of skeletons, perhaps as many as a thousand, of Coelophysis, a small meat-eating dinosaur. So many complete animals buried together is very rare, and it makes Coelophysis one of the best known early dinosaurs. It lived near the end of the Triassic, when dinosaurs were spreading but did not yet dominate the land.

title: The Central Atlantic lava floods
place: Newark Basin, New Jersey, USA (lavas also in Morocco, Brazil and Europe)
evidenceNote: Tiny zircon crystals in the lavas contain uranium that decays to lead at a known rate, dating the eruptions to within tens of thousands of years.
text: As Pangaea began to tear apart, basalt lava flooded more than 7 million square kilometres of what are now eastern North America, north-west Africa, Brazil and south-west Europe: the largest known lava province on the continents. Dating shows it erupted in four pulses over about 600,000 years, beginning at the same time as the end-Triassic extinction.

sources.title: Marzoli et al. 1999, Science: Extensive 200-million-year-old continental flood basalts of the Central Atlantic Magmatic Province
Blackburn et al. 2013, Science: Zircon U-Pb geochronology links the end-Triassic extinction with the Central Atlantic Magmatic Province

title: The end-Triassic mass extinction
evidenceNote: Fossils vanish from rocks of this age worldwide and the same layers hold chemical signs of volcanic gases, but exactly how the eruptions killed is still argued.
text: One of the five great mass extinctions. Up to about half of marine species diversity was lost, and on land most large reptiles other than dinosaurs disappeared. Scientists agree the Central Atlantic eruptions were the trigger but dispute how they killed: carbon dioxide causing warming and acid oceans, a burst of methane, gases from magma baking buried sediments, or short, intense volcanic winters.

sources.title: Ruhl et al. 2011, Science: Atmospheric carbon injection linked to end-Triassic mass extinction
Capriolo et al. 2020, Nature Communications: Deep CO2 in the end-Triassic Central Atlantic Magmatic Province
Davies et al. 2017, Nature Communications: End-Triassic mass extinction started by intrusive CAMP activity
Olsen et al. 2022, Science Advances: Arctic ice and the ecological rise of the dinosaurs
Blackburn et al. 2013, Science: Zircon U-Pb geochronology links the end-Triassic extinction with the Central Atlantic Magmatic Province

title: The central Atlantic opens
place: Central Atlantic, between eastern North America and north-west Africa
evidenceNote: Rift valleys filled with lava and sediment line both coasts, and the age of the sea floor between them shows when the ocean began to widen.
text: The first ocean to split Pangaea. Rifting between North America and Africa began in the Late Triassic, about 225 to 200 million years ago, and during the Early to Middle Jurassic new sea floor started to form between them. This narrow central Atlantic separated the northern continents, Laurasia, from the southern ones, Gondwana. The South Atlantic did not open until the Cretaceous.

sources.title: USGS This Dynamic Earth: Historical perspective (break-up of Pangaea)

title: The Karoo-Ferrar lava floods
place: Lesotho and South Africa (matching lavas in Antarctica)
evidenceNote: The lava flows are dated by radioactive decay in their minerals, in both southern Africa and Antarctica.
text: Basalt lava poured out across southern Africa and Antarctica, which were then joined together, covering about 3 million square kilometres with more than 2.5 million cubic kilometres of rock. The eruptions mark the first stage in the break-up of the southern supercontinent Gondwana, and they happened at the same time as a crisis in the oceans, the Toarcian Oceanic Anoxic Event.

title: The Toarcian ocean crisis
evidenceNote: Black, carbon-rich shales of this age are found around the world; they form only where the sea floor has no oxygen.
text: Large parts of the ocean lost their oxygen about 183 million years ago, at the same time as the Karoo-Ferrar eruptions. Temperatures rose, the seas became more acidic and many marine species died out. Black mud built up on the stagnant sea floor and preserved fossils in remarkable detail, as in Germany's Posidonia Shale.

title: Gondwana begins to break up
place: Mozambique Channel, between Africa and Madagascar
evidenceNote: The oldest sea floor between Africa and Madagascar, and lavas along the old rift, date the first split.
text: The southern supercontinent Gondwana started to come apart in the Early Jurassic, soon after the Karoo eruptions. East Gondwana (Antarctica, Madagascar, India and Australia) began to pull away from Africa and South America, opening the first stretch of the Indian Ocean. Over the next 150 million years Gondwana's pieces became the southern continents we know today.

title: The Morrison Formation
place: Morrison, Colorado, USA (the formation spans the western United States)
evidenceNote: Volcanic ash layers within the formation have been dated by radioactive decay, bracketing the dinosaur beds.
text: A sheet of river and floodplain sediments covering about 1.5 million square kilometres of the western United States, and North America's most famous source of Jurassic dinosaurs. Stegosaurus, Allosaurus, Diplodocus, Apatosaurus and Brachiosaurus all come from it. Only a tiny fraction of the formation is exposed at the surface where fossil hunters can reach it.

sources.title: UC Museum of Paleontology: The Jurassic Period

title: Solnhofen and Archaeopteryx
evidenceNote: The fine limestone formed in still lagoons of latest Jurassic age, dated by the fossils it contains.
text: Fine limestone laid down in warm, salty lagoons cut off from the open sea by reefs. Almost nothing could live in the bottom water, so animals that fell or drifted in were buried undisturbed in soft mud. The most famous is Archaeopteryx, a feathered, winged animal about half a metre long that still had sharp teeth and a long bony tail like a dinosaur.

sources.title: UC Museum of Paleontology: Solnhofen Limestone

title: The Paraná-Etendeka lava floods
place: Serra Geral, southern Brazil (matching lavas at Etendeka, Namibia)
evidenceNote: Lavas of the same age and chemistry are found in Brazil and in Namibia, on opposite sides of the Atlantic.
text: Flood basalts erupted 136 to 132 million years ago over about a million square kilometres of South America, with a smaller matching patch in Namibia and Angola. The two areas were side by side when the lava flowed. They were torn apart as the South Atlantic opened, and now lie on opposite shores of the ocean.

title: The first flowering plants
evidenceNote: The oldest fossil flowers and flower pollen that scientists agree on come from Early Cretaceous rocks.
text: Flowering plants (angiosperms) first appear as fossils in the Early Cretaceous, about 130 to 125 million years ago. By about 100 million years ago they were diversifying fast, and by the end of the period they dominated most land vegetation. Today they make up about 90 percent of living plant species. Bees and other insects diversified alongside them.

sources.title: UC Museum of Paleontology: The Cretaceous Period

title: The South Atlantic opens
place: South Atlantic, between South America and Africa
evidenceNote: The sea floor gets steadily older from the mid-ocean ridge towards both coasts, recording how the ocean grew.
text: South America and Africa, joined since Gondwana formed, split apart during the Early to middle Cretaceous. The rift unzipped from south to north, so the ocean opened first in the far south and last between Brazil and West Africa. The matching coastlines that Alfred Wegener pointed to in 1912, when he proposed that continents drift, are the scar of this break.

sources.title: USGS This Dynamic Earth: Historical perspective (break-up of Pangaea)

title: The feathered dinosaurs of Liaoning
evidenceNote: Volcanic layers among the fossil beds contain minerals whose radioactive decay gives their age.
text: Lake beds and volcanic ash in north-east China preserve an Early Cretaceous community, the Jehol Biota, in remarkable detail. The fossils include dinosaurs with feathers, such as Sinosauropteryx, which showed that feathers were not unique to birds. Early birds, mammals, insects and plants are preserved alongside them.

title: Oceanic Anoxic Event 1a and a volcanic puzzle
place: Ontong Java Plateau, western Pacific (the long-suspected cause)
evidenceNote: Black, carbon-rich mud marks the event in sea-floor rocks worldwide; new dating of the volcanic plateau long blamed for it no longer fits.
text: In the Selli Event large parts of the ocean ran short of oxygen and black, carbon-rich mud built up on the sea floor. It was long blamed on the eruption of the Ontong Java Plateau, a vast pile of undersea lava in the western Pacific. In 2023 new argon dating by Davidson and colleagues made the plateau up to 10 million years younger, too young to be the cause, so the trigger is uncertain again.

sources.title: Davidson et al. 2023, Science: A younger and protracted emplacement of the Ontong Java Plateau

title: Oceanic Anoxic Event 2
evidenceNote: A layer of black shale one to two metres thick marks the event, and the metal osmium in it carries a volcanic fingerprint.
text: At the boundary between the Cenomanian and Turonian ages, near the hottest point of the Cretaceous, the oceans again lost much of their oxygen. A band of black shale called the Bonarelli Level records it. Osmium in the sediments shows a huge burst of volcanic activity just before the event began, the probable trigger. Many marine species died out.

sources.title: Turgeon and Creaser 2008, Nature: Cretaceous oceanic anoxic event 2 triggered by a massive magmatic episode
NOAA Climate.gov: What's the hottest Earth's ever been?

title: A sea across North America
place: Great Plains of North America (chalk beds in Kansas)
evidenceNote: Chalk, shale and the bones of sea reptiles lie across the middle of the continent, far from any modern coast.
text: High Cretaceous seas flooded the middle of North America, joining the Gulf of Mexico to the Arctic Ocean and splitting the continent into two main landmasses, Laramidia in the west and Appalachia in the east. At its largest the Western Interior Seaway was about 970 km wide, more than 3,200 km long and 760 metres deep. Its sea-floor chalk now lies under the Great Plains.

title: India leaves Madagascar
evidenceNote: Sea-floor ages and matching rocks on both sides show when the two landmasses parted.
text: India and Madagascar had broken away from the rest of Gondwana together. Between about 95 and 84 million years ago they split from each other. Madagascar stayed beside Africa, while India crossed the ocean at 9 to 20 cm a year, very fast for a continent, towards its collision with Asia. The granite islands of the Seychelles are a fragment left behind on the way.

sources.title: USGS This Dynamic Earth: The Himalayas, two continents collide

title: Were the dinosaurs already in decline?
evidenceNote: Counting species through time depends on how many fossil-bearing rocks of each age survive and have been searched, so the same bones can be read both ways.
text: Were dinosaurs fading before the asteroid struck? Statistical studies of the dinosaur family tree (Sakamoto and colleagues 2016; Condamine and colleagues 2021) find new species appearing more slowly than old ones died out, from about 76 million years ago or earlier. Others (Bonsor and colleagues 2020; Dean and colleagues 2025) find no real decline, only fewer rocks of the right age to search. The question is open.

sources.title: Sakamoto et al. 2016, PNAS: Dinosaurs in decline tens of millions of years before their final extinction
Condamine et al. 2021, Nature Communications: Dinosaur biodiversity declined well before the asteroid impact
Bonsor et al. 2020, Royal Society Open Science: Dinosaur diversification rates were not in decline prior to the K-Pg boundary
Dean et al. 2025, Current Biology: The structure of the end-Cretaceous dinosaur fossil record in North America

title: The Rocky Mountains rise
evidenceNote: Folded and faulted rock layers, and the sand and gravel shed from the rising ranges, date the mountain building.
text: A long episode of mountain building, the Laramide orogeny, raised the Rocky Mountains of western North America. It began 80 to 70 million years ago, in the Late Cretaceous, and ended between 55 and 35 million years ago; the exact dates are argued over. During the same time the Western Interior Seaway drained away from the middle of the continent.

title: Hell Creek: the last dinosaurs
place: Hell Creek, near Jordan, Montana, USA
evidenceNote: Volcanic ash in these rocks has been dated by radioactive argon, and a coal layer marks the boundary above which no dinosaur bones are found.
text: River and swamp deposits laid down in roughly the last two million years of the Cretaceous. They hold some of the last dinosaurs: Tyrannosaurus, Triceratops, the duck-bill Edmontosaurus and the armoured Ankylosaurus. The dinosaurs stop at the boundary layer at the top of the formation, where argon dating ties the extinction to the Chicxulub impact to within 32,000 years.

sources.title: UC Museum of Paleontology: The Mesozoic Era
Renne et al. 2013, Science: Time scales of critical events around the Cretaceous-Paleogene boundary

title: The Deccan Traps eruptions
evidenceNote: Two teams dated the lava pile with different radioactive clocks and reached different answers about when most of it erupted.
text: Lava flows more than 2 km thick, covering about 500,000 square kilometres of western India, erupted across the end of the Cretaceous. Uranium-lead dating by Schoene and colleagues finds a large pulse starting tens of thousands of years before the asteroid impact; argon dating by Sprain and colleagues puts about three quarters of the lava after it. How much the eruptions added to the extinction is disputed.

sources.title: Schoene et al. 2019, Science: U-Pb constraints on pulsed eruption of the Deccan Traps
Sprain et al. 2019, Science: The eruptive tempo of Deccan volcanism in relation to the Cretaceous-Paleogene boundary
Hull et al. 2020, Science: On impact and volcanism across the Cretaceous-Paleogene boundary

title: The Chicxulub impact
evidenceNote: The buried crater has been mapped and drilled, and a thin layer of its debris is found in rocks of exactly this age all over the world.
text: An asteroid about 10 km across struck where the coast of Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula is now, blasting a crater 180 to 200 km wide that today lies buried under about a kilometre of younger rock. Debris from the impact forms a thin layer found around the globe. Darkness and cold followed. Argon dating places the impact within 32,000 years of the mass extinction.

sources.title: Schulte et al. 2010, Science: The Chicxulub asteroid impact and mass extinction at the Cretaceous-Paleogene boundary
Renne et al. 2013, Science: Time scales of critical events around the Cretaceous-Paleogene boundary
Morgan et al. 2016, Science: The formation of peak rings in large impact craters

title: The end-Cretaceous mass extinction
evidenceNote: Fossils of dinosaurs, ammonites and many plankton stop at the same thin layer of impact debris worldwide; what is argued is how much volcanoes added to the damage.
text: About three quarters of plant and animal species died out, including every dinosaur except the birds, the pterosaurs, the great sea reptiles and the ammonites. Most researchers hold that the Chicxulub impact was the main cause (Schulte 2010; Hull 2020; Chiarenza 2020). Others argue that the Deccan eruptions also drove the crisis (Schoene 2019). Mammals, birds, crocodiles and turtles came through.

sources.title: Schulte et al. 2010, Science: The Chicxulub asteroid impact and mass extinction at the Cretaceous-Paleogene boundary
Hull et al. 2020, Science: On impact and volcanism across the Cretaceous-Paleogene boundary
Chiarenza et al. 2020, PNAS: Asteroid impact, not volcanism, caused the end-Cretaceous dinosaur extinction
Schoene et al. 2019, Science: U-Pb constraints on pulsed eruption of the Deccan Traps
UC Museum of Paleontology: The Cretaceous Period

title: The North Atlantic lava floods
place: Giant's Causeway, Northern Ireland (lavas also in Scotland and Greenland)
evidenceNote: The lavas on both sides of the North Atlantic have been dated by radioactive argon in their minerals.
text: As Greenland began to tear away from Europe, lava flooded at least 1.3 million square kilometres in two main phases, about 62 to 58 and 56 to 54 million years ago. The basalt columns of the Giant's Causeway and Fingal's Cave are remnants. The second phase coincided with a sudden global warming, the Paleocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum, and may have triggered it.

sources.title: Storey et al. 2007, Science: Paleocene-Eocene thermal maximum and the opening of the Northeast Atlantic
Gutjahr et al. 2017, Nature: Very large release of mostly volcanic carbon during the Palaeocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum

title: The Paleocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum
place: Bighorn Basin, Wyoming, USA (a detailed record on land)
evidenceNote: Sea-floor mud and land sediments of this age show a sharp shift in carbon and oxygen isotopes, the chemical signature of a sudden release of carbon and a jump in temperature.
text: In less than 10,000 years the average global temperature rose by about 5 to 8 °C, to as high as 34 °C, and it stayed high for about 200,000 years. Thousands of billions of tonnes of carbon entered the air and the oceans. The source is debated: volcanic activity as the North Atlantic opened, or methane released from the sea floor. It is often seen as the closest ancient parallel to modern warming.

sources.title: NOAA Climate.gov: What's the hottest Earth's ever been?
Gutjahr et al. 2017, Nature: Very large release of mostly volcanic carbon during the Palaeocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum
Storey et al. 2007, Science: Paleocene-Eocene thermal maximum and the opening of the Northeast Atlantic

title: The North Atlantic opens
place: Norwegian Sea, between Greenland and Norway
evidenceNote: Lavas erupted at the moment of break-up, in East Greenland and beneath the sea, have been dated by radioactive argon.
text: The last major split of Pangaea's northern half. Greenland, still attached to North America, separated from north-west Europe about 55.5 million years ago and sea floor began to spread between them, opening the Norwegian Sea and completing the Atlantic Ocean. Until then, land animals could cross between Europe and North America by way of Greenland.

sources.title: Storey et al. 2007, Science: Paleocene-Eocene thermal maximum and the opening of the Northeast Atlantic
UC Museum of Paleontology: The Eocene Epoch

title: India collides with Asia
evidenceNote: The last sea-floor rocks caught between the continents and the slowing of India's drift each give a slightly different date for first contact.
text: After crossing the ocean from Gondwana, India ran into Asia and began to push up the Himalayas. Many accounts date first contact to about 55 million years ago; the US Geological Survey gives 50 to 40. Van Hinsbergen and colleagues argue that a smaller Tibetan-Himalayan fragment arrived about 50 million years ago, and that the main Indian continent collided only 25 to 20 million years ago.

sources.title: USGS This Dynamic Earth: The Himalayas, two continents collide
van Hinsbergen et al. 2012, PNAS: Greater India Basin hypothesis and a two-stage Cenozoic collision between India and Asia

title: The Green River lakes
evidenceNote: Volcanic ash layers in the lake beds have been dated by radioactive decay, and thin yearly layers of mud count off the time between them.
text: Large freshwater lakes lay across what is now south-west Wyoming and neighbouring states in the warm early Eocene. Their fine mud preserved fish in huge numbers, along with stingrays, palm leaves and many other plants and animals. The layers, laid down year by year, record about six million years. They show a subtropical Wyoming at the warmest time of the last 66 million years.

sources.title: US National Park Service: Fossils, Fossil Butte National Monument
UC Museum of Paleontology: Green River Formation
NOAA Climate.gov: What's the hottest Earth's ever been?

title: The Azolla event
evidenceNote: A drill core from the Arctic sea floor contains layers packed with the remains of the freshwater fern Azolla.
text: For about 800,000 years the Arctic Ocean, then almost enclosed and at times capped by fresh water, was covered again and again by mats of the floating fern Azolla. As the ferns died they sank and were buried, locking away carbon. Some researchers think this helped lower carbon dioxide and begin the long cooling from the Eocene hothouse; that link is still a hypothesis.

sources.title: Brinkhuis et al. 2006, Nature: Episodic fresh surface waters in the Eocene Arctic Ocean

title: The Messel Pit
evidenceNote: The oil shale formed on the bottom of a lake in a volcanic crater, and the volcanic rock has been dated by radioactive decay.
text: A lake in an old volcanic crater whose bottom mud turned to oil shale and preserved plants, insects and backboned animals in exceptional detail. Finds include bats, early horses and the primate Darwinius. Messel is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of the best windows anywhere on life in the warm middle Eocene.

sources.title: UC Museum of Paleontology: The Eocene Epoch

title: The Drake Passage opens
place: Drake Passage, between South America and Antarctica
evidenceNote: Estimates come from sea-floor ages, which are hard to read here, and from chemical traces of Pacific water in Atlantic sea-bed mud.
text: The sea passage between South America and Antarctica completes the ring of open ocean around Antarctica. When it opened is uncertain: estimates range from 49 to 17 million years ago. Scher and Martin found chemical traces of Pacific water reaching the Atlantic about 41 million years ago, which suggests a shallow early opening, with a deeper passage developing later.

sources.title: Scher and Martin 2006, Science: Timing and climatic consequences of the opening of Drake Passage

title: Whales with legs: Wadi al-Hitan and the Fayum
place: Wadi al-Hitan and the Fayum, Egypt
evidenceNote: The bones lie in sea-floor and river sediments dated by their fossils and by flips of Earth's magnetic field recorded in the rock.
text: In Egypt's Western Desert, Wadi al-Hitan ('Valley of the Whales') holds hundreds of fossils of early whales such as Basilosaurus and Dorudon, about 40 million years old. They still had small hind legs, feet and toes: proof that whales descend from land mammals. Younger river deposits in the nearby Fayum contain early relatives of monkeys and apes, such as Aegyptopithecus.

title: Australia leaves Antarctica
place: Southern Ocean, between Australia and Antarctica
evidenceNote: Sea-floor ages south of Australia record the widening gap between the two continents.
text: Australia was the last large piece of Gondwana to leave Antarctica. The two finally separated about 40 to 30 million years ago, and Australia then moved quickly north, as India had done before it. Cut off from the other continents, its marsupials and other animals evolved in isolation for tens of millions of years.

sources.title: Scher et al. 2015, Nature: Onset of Antarctic Circumpolar Current 30 million years ago as Tasmanian Gateway aligned with westerlies

title: Antarctica freezes over
evidenceNote: Oxygen isotopes in sea-floor shells shift sharply at this time, showing both colder water and a great volume of water locked up as ice.
text: At the boundary between the Eocene and Oligocene a continent-wide ice sheet grew on Antarctica and sea level fell by about 55 metres. The older explanation was that new sea passages let a cold current isolate the continent. Climate modelling by DeConto and Pollard points instead to falling carbon dioxide as the main cause, with the passages playing a secondary part.

sources.title: DeConto and Pollard 2003, Nature: Rapid Cenozoic glaciation of Antarctica induced by declining atmospheric CO2
Miller et al. 2020, Science Advances: Cenozoic sea-level and cryospheric evolution

title: The Tasmanian Gateway and the circumpolar current
place: South Tasman Rise, south of Tasmania
evidenceNote: The old edges of the continents show when deep water could first pass, and a chemical tracer in sea-bed mud shows when water from different oceans began to mix.
text: Deep water first flowed between Australia and Antarctica 33.5 million years ago, give or take 1.5 million years. By about 30 million years ago the gap had drifted into the belt of strong westerly winds, and the Antarctic Circumpolar Current, today the world's mightiest ocean current, began to circle the continent. It probably helped to keep carbon dioxide low afterwards.

sources.title: Scher et al. 2015, Nature: Onset of Antarctic Circumpolar Current 30 million years ago as Tasmanian Gateway aligned with westerlies

title: The Alps rise
dateLabel: from c. 55 million years ago; fastest c. 34–23 million years ago
evidenceNote: Rocks that formed on the floor of a vanished sea are now folded and stacked high in the mountains.
text: As Africa moved north it squeezed the Tethys Ocean shut and pressed smaller plates into the southern edge of Europe. The main phases of mountain building began in the Paleocene and Eocene, and the Alps were rising quickly during the Oligocene. The same long collision zone continues east to the Himalayas, and parts of it are still active today.

title: Riversleigh
evidenceNote: The fossil-bearing limestones are placed in order by the kinds of mammals they hold, compared with dated sites elsewhere.
text: Limestone in north-west Queensland holds Australia's most famous fossil record of mammals, running from the late Oligocene, about 28 million years ago, through the Miocene. It preserves relatives of koalas and thylacines, bats, birds and reptiles, many known from nowhere else, and shows how the wildlife of an isolated continent changed over millions of years. It has been a World Heritage Site since 1994.

title: The Himalayas and Tibet rise
dateLabel: from c. 50 million years ago; high by c. 23 million years ago
evidenceNote: Sea fossils in rocks of the high plateau show they formed under the Tethys Sea, and isotopes in ancient sediments record how high the land stood.
text: India's continuing push into Asia crumpled the crust into the Himalayas, 2,900 km long, and raised the Tibetan Plateau. Isotope records suggest the plateau stood about 3,000 metres high around 23 million years ago. Major phases of Himalayan mountain building in the Miocene changed Asia's monsoons. The range is still rising by more than a centimetre a year.

sources.title: USGS This Dynamic Earth: The Himalayas, two continents collide

title: The Columbia River lava floods
place: Columbia Plateau, Washington and Oregon, USA
evidenceNote: Each lava flow can be dated by radioactive argon in its minerals.
text: The youngest and one of the best preserved of Earth's great lava floods covered more than 210,000 square kilometres of Oregon, Washington, Idaho and Nevada. Nearly all of it erupted between 17 and 14 million years ago, most of it between 16.7 and 15.9. That matches a warm spell called the Miocene Climatic Optimum, and gases from the eruptions are thought to be its main cause.

title: The middle Miocene cooling
evidenceNote: Oxygen isotopes in sea-floor shells shift again, recording colder water and more ice on land.
text: After the warm Miocene Climatic Optimum, about 17 to 14 million years ago, the climate cooled sharply. The East Antarctic ice sheet grew again and has been permanent since about 12.8 million years ago. The cooler, drier world favoured open country over forest, and a wave of extinctions followed among species suited to the warmth.

sources.title: Miller et al. 2020, Science Advances: Cenozoic sea-level and cryospheric evolution

title: The Andes reach their height
dateLabel: mostly within the last 10 million years
evidenceNote: The ages of folded rocks and of valleys cut into the plateau's edge show when each part of the range rose.
text: The Andes formed where the floor of the Pacific, the Nazca Plate, slides beneath South America. Mountain building there has gone on for a very long time, but it had its greatest effect in the Miocene. The Altiplano, the high plateau around Lake Titicaca, is estimated to have risen 2,000 to 3,000 metres in the last ten million years, to more than 3,000 metres above the sea.

title: Tropical grasslands spread
evidenceNote: The chemistry of fossil teeth and ancient soils changes when animals switch from eating leaves to eating tropical grasses.
text: Grasses had been moving into open country since the Oligocene. Between about 7 and 6 million years ago grasses that use a more efficient kind of photosynthesis, called C4, expanded to become a major part of the world's vegetation in warm regions. Grazing mammals diversified with them. The oldest known upright-walking apes lived in Africa at about the same time.

sources.title: Brunet et al. 2002, Nature: A new hominid from the Upper Miocene of Chad, Central Africa

title: The Mediterranean dries out
place: Mediterranean basin (salt deposits in Sicily and beneath the sea floor)
evidenceNote: Drill cores from beneath the Mediterranean sea floor brought up thick layers of salt and gypsum, which form only when sea water evaporates.
text: Movements of the Earth's crust closed the sea passages linking the Mediterranean to the Atlantic. Cut off, the sea lost more water by evaporation than rivers could replace, and it partly or almost completely dried out, perhaps several times, leaving thick layers of salt on its floor. The episode is called the Messinian salinity crisis.

sources.title: Garcia-Castellanos et al. 2009, Nature: Catastrophic flood of the Mediterranean after the Messinian salinity crisis

title: The Zanclean flood
evidenceNote: A channel about 200 km long and more than 250 metres deep, cut into the sea bed through the strait, is thought to be the scar left by the flood.
text: The Atlantic broke through at Gibraltar and refilled the Mediterranean. A model based on the channel it carved suggests that, after a slow start, 90 percent of the water poured in within a few months to two years, at about a thousand times the flow of the Amazon, raising the sea by more than ten metres a day at the peak. The flood marks the start of the Pliocene.

sources.title: Garcia-Castellanos et al. 2009, Nature: Catastrophic flood of the Mediterranean after the Messinian salinity crisis

title: The Isthmus of Panama forms
evidenceNote: Rocks, fossils of sea creatures on either side, and DNA differences between Pacific and Caribbean species each record when the seaway closed, and they do not all agree.
text: Rising land finally joined North and South America and separated the Pacific from the Caribbean. A large review led by O'Dea in 2016 puts the complete land bridge at about 2.8 million years ago. Montes and colleagues, studying river sands in Colombia, argue the seaway had already closed by the middle Miocene, millions of years earlier, and Bacon and colleagues find early waves of migration. The date is still disputed.

sources.title: O'Dea et al. 2016, Science Advances: Formation of the Isthmus of Panama
Montes et al. 2015, Science: Middle Miocene closure of the Central American Seaway
Bacon et al. 2015, PNAS: Biological evidence supports an early and complex emergence of the Isthmus of Panama

title: The Great American Interchange
evidenceNote: South American animals appear in North American fossil beds from this time on, and northern animals appear in the south.
text: Once land joined the Americas, animals walked across in both directions. Ground sloths, armadillos, opossums, porcupines and giant flightless 'terror birds' went north; cats, horses, tapirs and many others went south. A few had crossed earlier, probably over water, but the exchange sped up dramatically about 2.7 million years ago. Many of South America's unique native mammals later died out.

sources.title: Woodburne 2010, Journal of Mammalian Evolution: The Great American Biotic Interchange

title: Ice sheets grow in the north
evidenceNote: Sea-floor cores from the far North Pacific record colder winters and more floating ice from this time on.
text: After millions of years of slow cooling, large ice sheets began to grow on the northern continents about 2.7 million years ago. From then on the ice advanced and retreated in step with small, regular changes in Earth's orbit and tilt: about every 41,000 years at first and, after roughly a million years ago, about every 100,000 years. This is the ice age we still live in.

sources.title: Haug et al. 2005, Nature: North Pacific seasonality and the glaciation of North America 2.7 million years ago
Miller et al. 2005, Science: The Phanerozoic record of global sea-level change

title: The ice-age giants die out
evidenceNote: Radiocarbon dates on the last bones of each species are compared with the dates of human arrival and of climate swings, and the match differs from region to region.
text: Mammoths, giant ground sloths, sabre-toothed cats and most other very large animals died out: about 65 percent of large species worldwide, and more than 80 percent in South America and Australia. Many researchers blame hunting and other pressure from spreading humans (Sandom 2014; Svenning 2024). Others point to rapid climate swings (Cooper 2015; Stewart 2021) or to both together.

Svenning et al. 2024, Cambridge Prisms: Extinction: The late-Quaternary megafauna extinctions
Cooper et al. 2015, Science: Abrupt warming events drove Late Pleistocene Holarctic megafaunal turnover
Stewart et al. 2021, Nature Communications: Climate change, not human population growth, correlates with Late Quaternary megafauna declines in North America
UC Museum of Paleontology: The Pleistocene Epoch

title: The La Brea Tar Pits
place: Rancho La Brea, Los Angeles, California, USA
evidenceNote: The bones are young enough to be dated by radiocarbon, which measures the decay of carbon-14 in once-living tissue.
text: Natural asphalt seeping to the surface in what is now Los Angeles trapped animals for tens of thousands of years. The collections cover the last 50,000 years and more than 660 species; the commonest large mammals are dire wolves, sabre-toothed cats and coyotes. A 2023 study of dated bones found the big mammals there had vanished by about 13,000 years ago, at a time of warming, more people and large fires.

sources.title: La Brea Tar Pits and Museum: Mammal collections
UC Museum of Paleontology: La Brea Tar Pits

title: The Last Glacial Maximum
evidenceNote: Ridges of debris left by the ice are dated by radiocarbon and by how long their boulders have been exposed, and old shorelines and corals show how far the sea fell.
text: The most recent peak of the ice age. Ice sheets covered Canada, Scandinavia and much of Britain: about a quarter of all land. So much water was locked up as ice that the sea stood 125 to 134 metres lower, exposing land bridges such as Beringia between Siberia and Alaska. The global average temperature was about 6 °C lower than before industry.

sources.title: Clark et al. 2009, Science: The Last Glacial Maximum
Lambeck et al. 2014, PNAS: Sea level and global ice volumes from the Last Glacial Maximum to the Holocene
Tierney et al. 2020, Nature: Glacial cooling and climate sensitivity revisited

title: The Younger Dryas cold snap
evidenceNote: Yearly layers in Greenland ice record the sudden cooling and warming; the markers claimed as proof of an impact were not found when independent laboratories tested for them.
text: As the ice age was ending, the Northern Hemisphere swung back to near-glacial cold for about 1,200 years, then warmed abruptly into the Holocene. Most researchers link it to a disruption of the Atlantic's heat-carrying currents. Firestone, Kennett and colleagues proposed instead that a comet struck or exploded about 12,900 years ago; this impact hypothesis has been widely rejected, because independent tests failed to confirm its evidence.

sources.title: Firestone et al. 2007, PNAS: Evidence for an extraterrestrial impact 12,900 years ago
Kennett et al. 2009, Science: Nanodiamonds in the Younger Dryas boundary sediment layer
Holliday et al. 2016, PLoS One: A blind test of the Younger Dryas Impact Hypothesis

title: The Anthropocene: proposed and rejected
evidenceNote: Mud layers in the lake record plutonium from hydrogen-bomb tests from 1952; the argument is whether so recent a marker should define a formal unit of geological time.
text: Is there a new epoch made by humans? The Anthropocene Working Group proposed one beginning in 1952, marked by bomb-test plutonium in the mud of Crawford Lake. In March 2024 the Subcommission on Quaternary Stratigraphy voted the proposal down, 12 to 4, and the ICS and IUGS confirmed the decision. Officially we still live in the Holocene; 'Anthropocene' remains an informal word for the age of human impact.
